name: Neo-Marxism
summary: Neo-Marxism covers twentieth-century schools that keep Marx's critique of capitalism and class power but revise orthodox economics and determinism, adding culture, psychology, ideology and Weberian ideas of status and power. It explains why capitalism has persisted through consumer integration, hegemony and Keynesian management, and looks to varied agents of change rather than the industrial working class alone. Its economic strands stress monopoly capital, imperialism and dependency, and it generally rejects both liberal capitalism and Soviet-style state socialism.
scope: The mainstream of Western Marxism and its offshoots as presented in reference works: the Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, early Habermas), Gramsci's hegemony theory, and the monopoly-capital and dependency/world-systems strands (Baran, Sweezy, Amin, Wallerstein). Excludes Leninist and Maoist orthodoxy and purely analytical Marxism's rational-choice methods, which are noted where they differ. Many positions on modern issues are inferred.

keyFigures.name: Antonio Gramsci

keyFigures.name: Theodor W. Adorno

universal-healthcare.rationale: Neo-Marxists treat access to basic needs as a social right that markets deny to low-wage workers, so public provision follows from their critique of capitalism; healthcare itself is not a central text topic.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The tradition describes low-wage workers as exploited and wants better conditions, though most would call wage floors palliative rather than a cure for wage labour.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Neo-Marxist economics stresses monopoly and oligarchy in capitalism and the surplus it wastes, rejecting the claim that markets allocate better than collective decision.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Concentrated wealth and monopoly surplus are the core diagnosis, so sharply higher taxes on the wealthy follow as a minimum measure.

unions-good.rationale: Unions organise workers against capital and are welcomed, though Frankfurt theorists doubted that integrated unions remained radical.

property-fundamental.rationale: The tradition inherits Marx's critique of private ownership of the means of production, and sees property as a source of exploitation rather than a basic right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Neo-Marxists see monopoly corporations as a driver of exploitation and militarism and would constrain them, though many hold regulation cannot fix the system.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare cuts would worsen the exploitation of low-wage workers and minorities that neo-Marxists describe, so adherents strongly oppose them.

worker-ownership.rationale: Overcoming alienation and exploitation points to workers controlling production; Gramsci's early support for factory councils is the clearest source.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Marcuse describes administered society absorbing dissent and eliminating opposition, so adherents distrust state surveillance as a tool of control.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Adherents are split: Marcuse's discriminating tolerance favours curbing reactionary speech, while others defend open critical discourse.

strong-leader.rationale: Gramsci's party leads through building consent and a disciplined organisation, not a leader bypassing gridlock; the tradition is wary of authoritarian personalism after fascism.

state-harmful.rationale: Most neo-Marxists see the state as a field of class struggle to be captured and transformed, not as simply unnecessary and harmful; the withering away is a distant goal.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: The state's coercive apparatus is seen as the armour protecting class hegemony, so adherents would not expand it.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Marxist feminist strands split between treating sex work as exploitation to abolish and as labour to be protected.

decide-locally.rationale: Gramsci's councils favoured grassroots control, but neo-Marxists also stress national and international structures of capital, so the tradition is genuinely split.

traditional-family.rationale: Critical theory examined the family as an agency of authority and ideology, so adherents do not treat traditional family structure as society's foundation.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Marcuse's critique of repression of Eros and the Marxist feminist strands support sexual liberation, though marriage as an institution is treated critically.

abortion-legal.rationale: The feminist strands of neo-Marxism support reproductive autonomy as part of ending women's subordination.

more-religion-public.rationale: Gramsci treated religion as a vehicle of traditional intellectuals and conservative common sense; critical theory is secular and sceptical of its public role.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The tradition applies class analysis to exploited minorities and extends critique to race, so it supports active correction of historical injustice.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Gramsci saw national culture as contested terrain of hegemony, and the tradition prioritises class and international solidarity over preservation of tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: The tradition aims at transforming society, with Marcuse's Great Refusal; though Gramsci's war of position is slow, it is not deference to established institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Class internationalism and focus on exploited minorities lead adherents to oppose restricting immigration.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theorists see international bodies as dominated by core powers, while internationalism favours cooperation; adherents are split.

free-trade.rationale: Dependency and world-systems strands treat trade as an unequal exchange that exploits peripheral nations.

nation-first.rationale: Neo-Marxism is internationalist in analysis and sympathies, although anti-imperialist strands back the self-assertion of dominated nations.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Baran and Sweezy see Western military spending as imperialist, and adherents distrust claims of humanitarian motive.

limit-growth.rationale: Marcuse criticises consumerist needs and waste but envisions abundance freed from toil; adherents are divided.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Marcuse holds that technology is not neutral and that technological rationality has become political domination, so adherents reject naive faith in progress.

expand-nuclear.rationale: No stated position; adherents are split between planning-based support and anti-militarist suspicion.

revolution-justified.rationale: Neo-Marxists retain the goal of transforming capitalism, though Habermas and Gramsci favour non-insurrectional paths, so agreement is moderate.

experts-over-public.rationale: Critical theory criticises instrumental reason and technocratic domination, and Gramsci wants workers' own organic intellectuals.

central-planning.rationale: Baran's planned surplus concept assumes a rationally planned socialist economy, though many neo-Marxists criticise Soviet-style planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Analytical Marxists and many others accept markets under social or worker ownership, and the statement permits only that, not capitalism.

basic-income.rationale: Marxists split between seeing basic income as freeing people from wage compulsion and as a reformist concession to capitalism.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Dependency theory supports protecting peripheral industry, but protectionism in rich countries is seen as nationalist; split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Neo-Marxists criticise capitalist investment decisions and support socially directed investment, via planning or a state aligned to workers.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The aim is social ownership of the means of production, not distribution among small owners.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: It is the classic Marxist long-run goal, but neo-Marxists rarely foreground it and many treat it as distant.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The tradition rejects market-led money and wants democratic control of finance, not its abandonment to markets.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Marcuse regards integration of labour and business under a strong state as a sign of one-dimensional domination, not of democracy.

one-party-rule.rationale: Western Marxists broadly criticise Soviet single-party rule; Gramsci's party is a hegemonic leader within civil society, and Frankfurt theorists favour critical independence.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Hereditary rule contradicts the egalitarian, emancipatory aims of the tradition.

democracy-best.rationale: Critical theory criticises existing democracy as hollowed out, but endorses democratic self-rule in principle; the clause about voters choosing badly makes agreement qualified.

direct-votes.rationale: Gramsci's councils and the New Left favoured participatory democracy, but no direct position is stated on referendums.

workers-councils.rationale: Gramsci backed factory councils as workers' self-rule in 1919-1920, though later he emphasised the party, so it is a leading but not exclusive view.

natural-rulers.rationale: The egalitarian tradition rejects innate fitness to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: Marcuse backed the Great Refusal and revolution is justified in principle, but Adorno and Habermas stress non-violence, so disagreement is moderate.

war-builds-character.rationale: Baran and Sweezy see war and militarism as outlets for capitalist surplus, and the tradition is anti-militarist.

separate-church-state.rationale: Gramsci criticised the church's hold on civil society through traditional intellectuals; secularism is the default.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion as a source of conservative common sense contradicts the rational critical stance of the tradition.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Privatising coercive functions would deepen class power, contradicting the tradition.

military-superiority.rationale: Baran and Sweezy criticise militarism as imperialist surplus absorption.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The tradition is internationalist and sides with exploited minorities, so it rejects ethnic homogeneity as an aim.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Class conflict remains the central category for neo-Marxists, even where they add status, culture and power as in Weberian-influenced strands.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Critique of class inequality and exploitation points to equality of outcomes, not merely of opportunity.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theory treat the periphery's underdevelopment as the product of core exploitation, supporting redress.

civilizational-union.rationale: The tradition organises around class and global systems, not religion or civilization.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Marcuse criticises needs manufactured by consumer society and individualist ideology, and the tradition stresses solidarity.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Marcuse's new sensibility changes the relation to nature, but the tradition has no consensus on intrinsic value.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Marcuse criticises the technological apparatus's domination but sees industrial productivity as the potential basis of freedom.

human-enhancement.rationale: No stated position; Marcuse's liberation of the body is balanced by suspicion of technological control.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Critical theory's critique of instrumental reason and administered society rejects handing governance to algorithms.

restore-past-order.rationale: The tradition is a project of emancipation through critique and transformation, and it opposes restoring older orders.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Horkheimer contrasts critical theory with traditional theory that takes the social order as given, so adherents resist ideologically neutral technocracy.

direct-action.rationale: Gramsci's war of position works through civil society and party organisation, Marcuse backed movements, and Habermas backed parliamentary routes; split.

means-match-ends.rationale: The New Left stressed prefigurative practice, while Gramsci favoured a disciplined party; adherents are split.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Marcuse looks to advanced productivity to free people from toil, so a return to foraging is contrary to the tradition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: It is a classic Marxist aim tied to alienation, but is not specifically developed by neo-Marxists.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Production for need is the Marxist communist aim, and neo-Marxists inherit it.

production-for-use.rationale: Marcuse and Baran object to production geared to profit and waste, rather than satisfying real needs.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Neo-Marxists retain the exploitation concept, though strands like analytical Marxism rework the labour theory underlying it, and dependency theory shifts exploitation to the international level.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Western Marxists tend to avoid or criticise the Leninist formula, emphasising democracy and consent.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Baran and Sweezy argue that monopoly capital's surplus flows into imperialist and militarist spending; war between powers is less emphasised than imperialism, so the statement is only partly matched.

taxation-theft.rationale: The tradition supports redistributive taxation and sees property rights claims as masking exploitation.

harm-principle.rationale: Marcuse accepts restrictions in the name of liberation, so adherents do not treat the harm principle as the only limit.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Class and group analysis, including attention to minorities and nations, leads adherents to reject an individual-only account of rights.

conscription.rationale: The tradition is anti-militarist, so it opposes state conscription for imperial wars.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Exit as a check is a market-liberal idea, opposed to the collective democratic emphasis of the tradition.

state-as-business.rationale: Governments run as businesses with customers is the market logic that neo-Marxists criticise.

positive-liberty.rationale: Marcuse's notion of freedom requires the real material possibility of different choices, and neo-Marxism criticises formal freedom without material means.

media-academia-power.rationale: Gramsci's civil society institutions shape consent, but adherents say capital rather than universities and media holds power, so the statement is split.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The tradition explains group differences by social and economic relations and rejects biological racial hierarchy; the overview does not address the genetics claim.

organic-representation.rationale: Corporatist representation through families and trade bodies is the integration that critical theory criticises.

total-state.rationale: Critical theory arose partly as a critique of totalitarianism and state capitalism, and the tradition rejects total control.

national-rebirth.rationale: Frankfurt theorists analysed national rebirth rhetoric as fascist, and the tradition rejects it.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Baran and Sweezy criticise imperialism, so adherents reject territorial expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal-style rule by personal oath is alien to and opposed by the tradition.

bound-labor.rationale: Opposed as a form of exploitation inherent in the tradition's analysis.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Horkheimer's critical theory holds that traditional theory reflects the social order, and Gramsci says culture and ideology are arenas of class power.

universal-morality.rationale: Frankfurt theory and Habermas offer universal norms through discourse, but Marxism's historicism challenges timeless moral truths; adherents are split, leaning to sceptical.

single-common-good.rationale: Neo-Marxists see society as divided by class interests, so one reasoned common good ignores conflict.

revive-national-language.rationale: No stated position; Gramsci wrote on language and culture, but there is no clear rule.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Gramsci's factory councils and Marxist critique of alienation at work support democratic control in firms.

school-vouchers.rationale: Vouchers are market mechanisms in education, opposed by an egalitarian, public-provision left.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Neo-Marxist economists borrow from post-Keynesians and see Keynesian spending as part of capitalism's workings, so oppose austerity.

economic-freedom.rationale: Marcuse says freedom in advanced capitalism is illusory and that economic freedom as capital's liberty does not secure political freedom.

national-self-determination.rationale: Dependency theory supports dominated nations' independence from neo-colonial control, though class interests complicate it.

force-without-un.rationale: The tradition criticises imperial military action by core powers, so it opposes unilateral force.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Critical theory is secular and rational, though its critique of instrumental reason limits the claim that reason is the only guide.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The tradition's class internationalism opposes excluding immigrant workers from welfare.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Coercive work requirements deepen compulsion to sell labour, which the tradition criticises.

class-collaboration.rationale: Neo-Marxism holds capital and labour to have opposed interests, so partnership is rejected, even though Marcuse worried that integration was occurring.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Adorno defended autonomous art and Benjamin was more open, but the tradition does not endorse destroying cultural institutions.

workers-nation.rationale: Marxism is internationalist, so adherents reject nation-based worker organisation.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Feminist neo-Marxists such as the social reproduction theorists reject legally fixed gender roles, and the wider tradition's egalitarianism points the same way.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Gramsci holds the state is hegemony protected by coercion, serving the dominant class, but neo-Marxists generally reject a crude instrumental view and stress relative autonomy.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Support for exploited minorities and anti-hegemonic cultural analysis opposes forced assimilation.

elite-replacement.rationale: Neo-Marxists explain migration through labour markets and global capitalism, which leaves no room for a replacement conspiracy; s1 does not address it.

national-mission.rationale: The tradition criticises imperialist spread of government forms by core powers.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The feminist strands of neo-Marxism treat patriarchy as a structural system of male advantage.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The tradition says elites serve ruling-class interests and are detached from workers, though it frames this as structural rather than moral corruption.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Frankfurt School analysed eugenic and fascist doctrines critically, and the tradition rejects them.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Support follows from the criticism of coercive state apparatuses, but not a core text statement.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Limited government protecting property is the liberal position neo-Marxism opposes.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Critical theory's emancipatory aim rests on equal dignity of all, though adherents critique formal legal equality as insufficient.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Western Marxists criticised Soviet socialism, but the question is mostly a debate of Leninist strands; split.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Anti-colonial analysis supports the claim, but it is not a central neo-Marxist topic.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Gramsci saw the state as an educator shaping a worldview, and a secular left supports no religious instruction in state schools.

trade-surplus.rationale: Core-periphery analysis rejects mercantilist export aims as beggar-thy-neighbour, but is not a central topic.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Libertarian non-aggression is not a Marxist principle; revolution and state coercion are accepted in some forms.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The tradition treats competition as capitalist ideology and emphasises cooperation and class conflict.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Marcuse's discriminating tolerance supports limits on reactionary movements, but many adherents distrust state bans of parties as used against the left.

separated-powers.rationale: Gramsci discussed separation of powers as part of the bourgeois state, with no settled neo-Marxist position.

vanguard-party.rationale: Gramsci's Modern Prince favoured a disciplined party, while Frankfurt School and council strands opposed vanguardism, so adherents are split.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The tradition's orientation is to exploited and low-wage workers and minorities.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: No stated position; privatising public housing is opposed by many but supported as asset ownership by some.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The tradition supports workers' collective action against capital, so adherents oppose restrictions.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Neo-Marxists attribute poverty to exploitation and unequal exchange, not population growth.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The tradition attributes social conflict to class and exploitation, and not to ethnic diversity.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Critical theory's experience of fascism makes adherents wary of emergency suspension of rights.

party-controls-media.rationale: Critical theory criticises control of media by both capital and the state; Habermas's public sphere requires independence.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Class internationalism and support for exploited minorities oppose lengthy barriers to citizenship.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Councils and Marx's Commune model support representatives paid worker-level wages, though neo-Marxists do not foreground it.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Gramsci endorsed democratic centralism, but New Left and Frankfurt strands rejected binding party discipline, so adherents are split.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Internationalist in principle but the EU is seen as a capitalist project; split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Concentrating command and ministerial choice in a head of state conflicts with the tradition's democratic collectivism.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Hierarchical church government is not a concern of the tradition, and adherents oppose clerical authority.

clerical-rule.rationale: Gramsci treats clerical intellectuals as traditional authorities to be displaced, and the tradition is secular.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Leninist revolutionary defeatism is not a neo-Marxist norm; Frankfurt theorists and others differ.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Adorno defended autonomous art, and critical theory opposes moralistic censorship.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall is a Commune and council-democracy feature, but not a neo-Marxist emphasis.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Baran and Sweezy's critique of militarism supports ending alliances, though the tradition does not state it directly.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Compulsory universal home-ownership is not a Marxist aim and would spread property; they favour social provision.

people-in-arms.rationale: Marxist tradition favours an armed people over a standing army, but neo-Marxists rarely address it.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Gramsci wants organic intellectuals tied to workers, but the tradition itself is academic and rejects the anti-intellectual claim.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Anti-colonial critique rejects hierarchy among cultures, while critical theory retains some universal standards; split.

death-penalty.rationale: The tradition opposes state killing, which falls hardest on the poor and minorities.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The feminist and liberationist strands support sex education and gender equality in schooling.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Marcuse criticised repressive desublimation but also repression of Eros; adherents and Marxist feminists are split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Descent-based citizenship conflicts with the tradition's internationalism.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Marcuse criticises one-dimensional conformity and the integration of dissent, aligned with Mill's concern for conformity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theory regard debt as a mechanism of neo-colonial exploitation.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The dependency strands' core argument is that formal independence leaves peripheral economic domination in place.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Marcuse and Western Marxists criticise both Soviet repression and developmental authoritarianism.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The tradition says rich countries owe redress for exploitation, though many see aid as itself a tool of dependence.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The tradition's critique of militarism opposes nuclear arming.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Insulating money from democratic control serves capital, and neo-Marxists oppose it.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The left usually backs negotiated settlements, but this is not a central issue.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The tradition goes further and rejects private productive property, but it clearly agrees property should serve social ends.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Pollock's state capitalism and Western Marxist critiques of the USSR support the view, though adherents differ on the label.

collective-defense.rationale: NATO-style alliances are seen as instruments of Western power, but the tradition does not address it directly.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The anti-imperialist stance supports the claim.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Gramsci saw church influence as a pillar of conservative hegemony, favouring curbing it.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The tradition wants progressive taxation to reduce inequality.

character-from-environment.rationale: Critical theory and the tradition emphasise social formation of character and consciousness over innate nature.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The tradition aims at democratic popular power rather than balancing few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: Western Marxists and Frankfurt theorists criticised Stalinist and fascist leader cults.

equal-parenting.rationale: Marxist feminists are split on shared-custody presumptions.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Maoist idea; Western Marxists are not bound to it and are split.

refugee-return.rationale: The left generally supports return rights, but it is not a central neo-Marxist subject.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Ethnic irredentism is nationalist, opposed by an internationalist tradition.

common-currency.rationale: Adherents split over the euro as a capitalist project versus internationalism.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Union by ancestry is a nationalist idea contrary to class internationalism.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Marxist debate on nationalities historically divided; no neo-Marxist consensus.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Gramsci rejected mechanical economic determinism and neo-Marxists stress culture and ideology, though they still ground change in material relations, so the answer is split.

ban-cartels.rationale: Neo-Marxists see monopoly as built into capitalism and doubt competition law can fix it, yet support controls on concentration, so the answer is split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Critical theory is wary of unconstrained majorities and the tradition values protection of minorities, though it also criticises courts as class instruments.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The feminist strands support quotas for equal representation.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: An autarkic bloc of a country and its colonies runs against the tradition's anti-imperialism; the overview does not address it.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding labour standards protect workers, though many see them as insufficient; support is moderate.

moral-incentives.rationale: Marxist-Guevarist idea not specific to neo-Marxism; split.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Gramsci rejected insurrectionary shortcuts in the West and favoured building consent, though Third Worldist strands differ.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Egalitarian aims require abolishing inherited privilege.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The tradition criticises nationalist education, which serves hegemony.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Imperialist tutelage is what the dependency and anti-colonial critique opposes.

patriotic-education.rationale: Gramsci treats schools as instruments of hegemony, and adherents oppose nationalist indoctrination.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The tradition supports correcting racial injustice and opposes ending preferences.

public-money-creation.rationale: Neo-Marxists with post-Keynesian leanings favour public control of money, but it is not a central position.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Neo-Marxism is defined by explaining capitalism's persistence through Keynesian policy and integration, in contrast to classical collapse theory.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Cultivating influence in former colonies is the neo-colonialism the tradition criticises.

delink-world-market.rationale: Amin advocated delinking from the world market while other neo-Marxists sought reform within the world system, so they are split.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Dependency theorists differ on whether workers in core countries share in imperial gains, so the answer is split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Habermas supports constitutional rights, but the tradition criticises formal bourgeois rights; split.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Anti-imperialist analysis supports rejecting unequal colonial settlements.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Neo-Marxists accept resistance to illegitimate rule, though their framing is class-based.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Gramsci and the councils placed popular power in workers' bodies, while Habermas supports parliamentary legitimacy; split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Marcuse's new sensibility and ecological strand lean to it, though animals are not a core Marxist topic.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The tradition says the wealthy owe structural redistribution, not paternal charity.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Critical theory is committed to engagement and transformation of society.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Gramsci's hegemony is rule by consent as well as force, and critical theory grounds legitimacy in discourse justifiable to all affected, though neo-Marxists say manufactured consent is not real consent.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Marcuse's integration thesis make this a defining claim of the tradition.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramsci's hegemony, the state as hegemony protected by the armour of coercion, is the signature concept of the strand.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theory treat exploitation as external between nations, as the article describes.

party-own-road.rationale: Western Marxism broke with Soviet-style orthodoxy and direction.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Anti-Eurocentric critiques are present but the tradition has no clear position; split.

filial-duty.rationale: Frankfurt School work on the authoritarian family critiques patriarchal duty, yet adherents also value solidarity; no settled position.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Its critique of capitalism and support for collective social provision oppose handing retirement security to private firms and markets.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Critical theory and the structural view of power treat unequal outcomes as evidence of systemic domination regardless of intent, though race is not the main focus of the founding texts.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: One-Dimensional Man argues that consumer integration and manufactured needs pacify people and sustain the system.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Anti-imperialism and the rejection of Soviet-style state socialism lead neo-Marxists to condemn military intervention in a bloc member, as with Czechoslovakia in 1968.

corporate-influence.rationale: Monopoly-capital and hegemony theory hold that capital shapes the state and political culture, so lobbying and campaign money are expressions of class power.

democratic-peace.rationale: Dependency and imperialism theorists see liberal 'democracy promotion' as cover for capitalist domination, and Marcuse questions whether liberal democracies are free.

non-intervention.rationale: Split: dependency theorists oppose imperialist intervention, but the tradition also backs solidarity with liberation movements and has no rule of absolute non-intervention.

industrial-unions.rationale: Neo-Marxists favour workers' organisation and councils (Gramsci's factory councils) but the strand takes no settled line on industrial versus craft unions.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy against the nation by a minority runs against the class analysis and the Frankfurt School's study of authoritarian prejudice and antisemitism.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marxist tradition criticises bourgeois marriage and property but neo-Marxists are split on abolishing legal marriage; the topic is peripheral to the sources.

informal-organisation.rationale: Gramsci stresses the party as the 'modern prince' and organised civil society in the war of position, against purely informal small-group struggle.

religious-nation.rationale: The tradition is secular and treats religion as ideology and part of hegemony; defining the nation by religion cuts against its class and cultural critique.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Neo-Marxists keep Marx's critique of private ownership of the means of production, not of personal belongings.

religion-illusion.rationale: Gramsci and the Frankfurt School treat religion as an ideology bound to social conditions that reproduces the existing order.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Neo-Marxism inherits Marx's view of capitalism as a stage that built productive forces, while stressing its persistence and harms.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Neo-Marxists reject both liberal capitalism and Soviet-style state socialism in favour of a revised socialism.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Critical Theory, especially Adorno, treats Auschwitz and its denial as central to the critique of modern society.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Marcuse and the Frankfurt School called for sexual liberation and criticised repressive sexual norms.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Critical of authoritarian repression, though Marcuse's 'repressive tolerance' argued for limiting some reactionary movements.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Dependency and world-systems strands argue that colonial and peripheral economies are structured to benefit the core.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Calls for democratisation of workplaces and society, and Habermas stresses public deliberation by citizens.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Critical theory links domination across class, culture and gender, though class remains the primary axis.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Holds that class conflict and domination structure politics, so merging left and right is rejected.

alienated-labor.rationale: Alienation under capitalism is a core theme carried over from Marx into the Frankfurt School and Marcuse.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Treats religion as ideology and locates authority in social relations and the people, not God.

social-market-economy.rationale: Marcuse argues advanced welfare capitalism integrates workers and masks domination, so a reformed market is not the goal.

rich-first.rationale: Opposes inequality and exploitation, so letting some grow rich first is rejected.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hereditary succession of power contradicts the Marxist critique of class privilege and the democratic aims of the Frankfurt and Gramscian traditions.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theorists (Amin, Wallerstein) argue that lender conditions entrench the periphery's subordination, so refusing them follows from the theory.

property-franchise.rationale: Neo-Marxists treat class power as the obstacle to democracy; wealth-based franchise embodies the bourgeois privilege they criticise.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Marcuse and later critical theory linked domination of nature to domination of people, and eco-feminist strands extend it; not universal across the schools.

reification.rationale: Reification is a core concept of Western Marxism from Lukacs through the Frankfurt School, which Marcuse and Adorno carried into their critique of consumer society.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Marcuse's critique of repressive tolerance and Gramsci's account of hegemony hold that ruling-class ownership of media and institutions hollows out formal freedoms.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Gramsci and the Frankfurt School criticised bourgeois legality as class rule but also valued the rule of law against authoritarianism; adherents split.

racial-franchise.rationale: Neo-Marxism is universalist and anti-racist, and the Frankfurt School analysed racial and fascist domination as a pathology to oppose.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a religious minority's shops is scapegoating that Frankfurt School studies of prejudice and authoritarianism condemn.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Neo-Marxism builds on Marx's critique of how capital concentration produces class power, and monopoly-capital theorists such as Baran and Sweezy stress that concentrated wealth dominates politics.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Neo-Marxists see police as part of the apparatus of class power, but abolition was not a program of the classical Frankfurt or Gramscian strands; adherents split.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Critical Theory grew out of analysing fascist mobilisation and authoritarian conformity, so drilled national youth organisations are opposed.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Marxist critique of capitalism holds that profit and rent from ownership are unearned claims on workers' labour, which these schools keep.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Marcuse defended a right of resistance to oppression, including violent liberation movements, so adherents do not hold killing in defence to be always wrong.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Critical Theory and Gramsci treat national narratives as ideology that serves ruling groups, so an unbroken national essence is rejected.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The tradition is materialist and explains politics through class, power and ideology rather than good and evil.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Neo-Marxism has no doctrine of national homelands and diasporas; adherents are indifferent or split.

culture-before-state.rationale: Gramsci's war of position holds that a counter-hegemony in culture and civil society must be built before the state can be won, though he speaks of classes, not nations.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Neo-Marxists criticise religion as ideology but support emancipation of women; no shared position on judging scripture exists.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The strand analyses class and imperialism and opposes privileging a national or ethnic majority in economic life.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Gramsci's factory councils and the neo-Marxist insistence on working-class self-emancipation make real working-class power the test of socialism.

family-wage.rationale: Marcuse and Marxists generally question wage labour itself, and a family wage is a traditional-family claim most neo-Marxists would not endorse.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Marcuse questioned technology's direction under capitalism, but the tradition never addressed ageing research.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Never addressed; Frankfurt School critique of surveillance favours privacy, but not specifically untraceable money.

person-over-state.rationale: The Frankfurt School's critical theory defends individual autonomy against domination by a totalising system, including the state.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The tradition is largely secular and materialist but stressed non-material needs; Marcuse's true needs concern more than material life.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Neo-Marxism centres class, not race, and generally rejects racial-group organising, though it supports anti-racism.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Neo-Marxists opposed imperialist wars and many wars of aggression but did not restrict force to defence alone; the tradition never addressed the question directly.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Dependency theory blames imperial economic domination rather than plots to partition countries; no stated position.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Ecological critique of capitalism is common, but many favor direct regulation or planning over pricing mechanisms; split.

capital-controls.rationale: Dependency and monopoly-capital strands see unrestricted capital flows as a tool of core-country dominance.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Collective organisation of workers is central to Marxist traditions, including Gramsci's factory councils.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Dependency and world-systems strands of neo-Marxism call for restructuring the world economy against rich-country extraction.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Neo-Marxism is split, as Gramsci favoured a war of position within civil society and the Frankfurt School doubted revolution, while some strands keep the revolutionary language.

sacred-nation.rationale: Neo-Marxism treats nationalism as ideology that obscures class, and the nation is not seen as sacred.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theory describe core regions exploiting peripheries, which is the same logic as internal colonialism.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Neo-Marxism is split, as Frankfurt critical theory keeps a notion of human potential and dignity while Marxist historicism treats human nature as historically made.

workers-own-party.rationale: Gramsci made the party the collective organiser of the subordinate classes, though the Frankfurt School was sceptical of party politics.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Gramsci wrote on language and hegemony but the tradition has no stated view on regional names, so it is split.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The strand criticizes formal elections as compatible with class hegemony and looks for substantive democracy beyond procedure.

premarital-sex.rationale: Marcuse and the Frankfurt School criticized sexual repression and favored sexual liberation.

women-suffrage.rationale: Equal political rights are a basic demand of the left tradition from which neo-Marxism comes.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Marxist critique treats property claims as the basis of class power, and ownership as social, so first claiming gives no rightful title.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: No stated doctrine; some dependency theorists see such courts as tools of imperial powers while others back international justice.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Secular critical tradition that treats religion as ideology to be critiqued, so literal inerrancy is rejected.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Rejects Soviet-style state socialism as bureaucratic domination, yet many opposed capitalist restoration; the strand is split.

indirect-election.rationale: Gramsci and others favoured council democracy but the Frankfurt School stressed direct participation; adherents are split.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Anti-colonial critique sees borders as imperial artefacts, yet no stated view on whether to redraw them; adherents split.

equal-conscription.rationale: No stated position; equality favours equal treatment but anti-militarism leans against any draft.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Gramsci made the party and civil-society organisations central to building hegemony, so bypassing them is rejected.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Marcuse holds technology is not neutral and serves domination; a return to ancestral values is not part of the strand, so this is an inference.

national-resource-control.rationale: The dependency and world-systems strands (Amin, Wallerstein) hold that foreign control of resources keeps poor countries dependent.

distribution-by-process.rationale: It treats unequal distribution as produced by capitalist class power, so fairness is judged by outcomes and structure, not the process of exchange.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Baran, Sweezy and others keep Marx's surplus theory, but the school as a whole revises orthodox economics, so it is contested.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Gramsci's national-popular idea links nation and workers, but other strands are internationalist, so adherents are split.

material-over-identity.rationale: The school adds culture, psychology and ideology to Marx's economics, so it does not put material interests above identity and cultural issues.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: It generally rejects Soviet-style state socialism and liberal capitalism, and does not endorse party-led market schemes.

police-more-powers.rationale: The state's coercive apparatus is seen as the armour protecting class hegemony, so adherents would not expand it. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: Mass culture and the media serve to pacify people and reproduce the existing social order.
missingStatements.rationale: Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Marcuse's integration thesis make this a defining claim of the tradition.

missingStatements.text: The ruling class maintains power mainly by winning the consent of the governed through culture and institutions, not only by force.
missingStatements.rationale: Gramsci's hegemony, the state as hegemony protected by the armour of coercion, is the signature concept of the strand.

missingStatements.text: Poor countries stay poor because the world economy is structured to transfer their surplus to rich countries.
missingStatements.rationale: Dependency and world-systems theory treat exploitation as external between nations, as the article describes.

notes: Neo-Marxism is a label applied from outside to diverse schools, and Frankfurt theorists themselves did not use it. Strands differ on revolution (Marcuse's Great Refusal, Gramsci's war of position, Habermas's gradualism), on the vanguard party, and on delinking. Many answers on modern issues are inferred from core principles and marked low confidence.
